question: I need a financial advisor to help me with my investments. Can you give me some insight?

answers:
Absolutely, I can help you with that. When looking for a financial advisor, consider the following:
1. They shouldn't try to sell you insurance first, as insurance is an expense, not an investment.
2. They should be able to explain the relationship between risk and return and recommend funds with good demonstrated returns after fees have been removed.
3. They should have a good track record, not just in terms of returns, but also in helping clients make the right investment choices, savings choices, tax-efficient choices, and expense choices. They should also help you stay disciplined and understand your true risk tolerance.
4. If you plan to pick your own funds, you might want to choose an online discount broker with the cheapest fees.
Remember, a financial advisor is not a necessity for everyone, especially if you're just starting out and your taxes are not complicated. However, if you have serious complications with your taxes or if you don't have the time or interest to manage your investments, a financial advisor could be beneficial.

evidence.text: Most individuals do not need a personal financial advisor. If you are soon entering the world of work, your discretionary investments should be focused on index funds that you commit to over the long run. Indeed, the best advice I would give to anyone just starting out would be: For most average young workers, a financial advisor will just give you some version of the information above, but will change you for it. I would not recommend a financial advisor as a necessity until you have seriously complicated taxes. Your taxes will not be complicated. Save your money.

Edit: You also seem to be talking about wealth managers.  I am talking about financial managers.  I believe very few wealth managers are actually worth their costs (and most are just blow horn prognosticators) whereas financial advisors are financial educators to clients.

If you don't have the time or interest to manage investments, you need a financial advisor.  Generally speaking, you're better served by an advisor who collects an annual fee based on a percentage of your account value. Advisors who are compensated based on transactions have a vested interest to churn your account, which is often not in your best interest. You also need to be wary of advisors who peddle expensive mutual funds with sales loads (aka kick-backs to the advisor) or annuities. Your advisor's compensation structure should be transparent as well.
